doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: New artists, Blue Note, and teaching at the New School
summary: He teaches two courses and urges students to be themselves.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: That’s just an example. That’s a good album man.
All right. I’ll be checking it out. And do you hear artists out there these days that you think are doing anything new?

That’s difficult for me to say because first of all, [sings] don’t get around much anymore. But if I do I’m on the outskirts of town. But just listening to the records or CD’s, or things, unfortunately no. Because I don’t know why Blue Note wants to recreate Art Blakey’s sound. You can’t. There’s no players that can — they can duplicate it but the feeling’s not there. So why not let these new, young artists do their own thing? You know what I mean? Give them their own voice. And therefore that question is difficult. Now I teach, I teach at the New School. I teach two classes down there, two courses. One is Rhythm Analysis and another one is Ensemble Improvisation. And there’s a lot of potential, talented young people down there. Hopefully every opportunity I have to confront them I try to instill in them, hey, be yourself. Do your thing. Don’t try to play like so-and-so and so-and-so. You play what you feel. Use your ideas. Use your thoughts. It’ll happen. So hopefully some of them will develop. But overall man, it’s like the people who originated this music, who originated this style, who originated this form, there’s no duplication. If a man shows you you can be like, you can play a lot, be like that, but it’s not the same. It’s just like Wynton Marsalis with the —
